note: Shared metric vectors: the cross-language ANSWER contract, replayed by both
Unlike canonical.json and receipts.json, this file is NOT generated. Those hold bytes
and signatures nobody can compute by hand, so a generator is the only way to author
them. Every number here was computed by hand from the metric's definition -- the
'hand' field on each case shows the arithmetic -- and then checked against the Python
implementation. Generating it from the code under test would make it a transcript of
whatever that code currently returns, which is exactly the shape of test that stays
green through the bug it exists to catch.
Python and TypeScript reach these answers by different routes: Python delegates to
trec_eval (via ir_measures) and scikit-learn, TypeScript counts them out against the
definitions. That is precisely why the pin has to exist. A divergence fails CI in
both languages rather than being discovered later by a human.

ranking.name: mixed_hits_at_3
ranking.hand: top-3 of (d1,d2,d3,d4,d5) holds d1 and d3. P=2/3. R=2/4 (denominator is the relevant SET of 4, never k). F1=2*(2/3)*(1/2)/((2/3)+(1/2))=(2/3)/(7/6). First hit is d1 at rank 1, so RR=1/1.

ranking.name: k_exceeds_the_returned_list
ranking.hand: 5 documents returned, k=10. 3 of the 4 relevant ones are in the list. P=3/10 -- the denominator is k, NOT min(k,5); the 5 positions the ranker never filled are charged for. R=3/4.

ranking.name: first_hit_at_rank_three
ranking.hand: the only relevant document x3 sits third. RR=1/3. P@4=1/4. R@4=1/1 -- the single relevant document was found.

ranking.name: nothing_relevant_was_retrieved
ranking.hand: the ranker returned none of the 2 relevant documents. P=0/3, R=0/2, RR=0 (a real zero: the ranker missed, and something WAS judged relevant). F1 takes the 0/0 branch and is 0, not NaN.

ranking.name: graded_gains_and_a_zero_gain_judgment
ranking.hand: gains a=3, b=2, c=1, d=0. A judged gain of 0 is judged NOT relevant, so the relevant set is {a,b,c} (size 3) and d is a miss. Ranked (d,c,a,e): top-2 holds only c, so P@2=1/2 and R@2=1/3. First hit is c at rank 2, so RR=1/2. Document e was never judged, which also means not relevant.

ranking.name: document_id_named_proto
ranking.hand: A document literally called '__proto__'. Relevant set is {__proto__, d2}, size 2. Top-2 of (__proto__, zz, d2) holds only __proto__, so P@2=1/2 and R@2=1/2, F1=2*(1/2)*(1/2)/1. First hit is at rank 1, so RR=1/1. This case exists because it once diverged: JavaScript's `plain['__proto__'] = 1` invokes Object.prototype's setter instead of creating a key, so the document vanished from the judgments and precision@1 was 1.0 in Python and 0 in the browser. Python has no such rule, and no refusal fired in either language -- both just answered, differently.

ranking.name: recall_denominator_is_the_relevant_set
ranking.hand: 10 relevant documents, the ranker returned 2 and both are relevant. P@2=2/2=1.0 (perfect) while R@2=2/10=0.2. The two must not collapse into one number: dividing recall by k would report 1.0 here and hide 8 misses.

ranking_refusals.name: k_is_zero
ranking_refusals.why: precision@0 divides by zero; the answer is undefined, not small

ranking_refusals.name: k_is_negative
ranking_refusals.why: a negative cut-off names no positions at all

ranking_refusals.name: ranked_list_repeats_a_document
ranking_refusals.why: refused, never de-duplicated: silently dropping the repeat changes both the positions and the count

ranking_refusals.name: relevance_gain_is_fractional
ranking_refusals.why: rounding 2.5 would move a document across the relevant boundary and no reference semantics says which way

ranking_refusals.name: relevance_gain_is_negative
ranking_refusals.why: a relevance grade is a level; there is no level below not-relevant

ranking_refusals.name: no_document_is_judged_relevant
ranking_refusals.why: recall has no denominator. Returning 0.0 would blame the ranker for missing JUDGMENTS -- a different failure with a different fix.

classification.name: perfect_separation
classification.hand: threshold 0.5 splits (0.1,0.2) from (0.8,0.9) exactly along the labels. tp=2, fp=0, tn=2, fn=0. accuracy=(2+2)/4, precision=2/2, recall=2/2, f1=1, fpr=0/(0+2), fnr=0/(0+2).

classification.name: one_error_of_each_kind
classification.hand: predictions at 0.5 are (0,1,0,1) against labels (0,0,1,1). tn=idx0, fp=idx1, fn=idx2, tp=idx3 -- one of every cell. accuracy=2/4, precision=1/2, recall=1/2, f1=2*(1/2)*(1/2)/1=1/2, fpr=1/(1+1), fnr=1/(1+1). This case is the one that catches a tp/fp transposition: every total still adds up under the swap, but fpr and fnr do not.

classification.name: threshold_moves_the_cells
classification.hand: same scores as above, threshold raised to 0.85: only 0.9 clears it, so predictions are (0,1,0,0). tp=0, fp=1, tn=1, fn=2. accuracy=1/4. precision takes the 0/0 branch -- nothing true was predicted positive out of 1 positive prediction, so 0/1=0. recall=0/2=0. f1 then takes the 0/0 branch and is 0, NOT NaN (scikit-learn's zero_division=0.0). fpr=1/(1+1), fnr=2/(2+0)=1.0 -- every positive was missed.

classification.name: score_equal_to_threshold_is_positive
classification.hand: both scores are exactly 0.5 at threshold 0.5. The comparison is >=, so BOTH are predicted positive: tp=1, fp=1, tn=0, fn=0. accuracy=1/2, precision=1/2, recall=1/1=1, f1=2*(1/2)*1/(3/2)=2/3, fpr=1/(1+0)=1.0, fnr=0/(0+1)=0. Flipping >= to > would make both predictions negative and every one of these six numbers change.

classification.name: imbalanced_screen_at_the_default_threshold
classification.hand: no threshold given, so the documented default 0.5 applies. 8 negatives, 2 positives. Scores over 0.5 are idx4 (0.55), idx5 (0.6) and idx9 (0.95). idx9 is the only true positive; idx4 and idx5 are false alarms; idx8 (0.45, label 1) is the miss. tp=1, fp=2, tn=6, fn=1. accuracy=(1+6)/10=0.7, precision=1/3, recall=1/2, f1=2*(1/3)*(1/2)/((1/3)+(1/2))=(1/3)/(5/6)=0.4, fpr=2/(2+6)=0.25, fnr=1/(1+1)=0.5. Accuracy 0.7 alongside recall 0.5 is why the cells are reported and not just the headline.

classification_refusals.name: length_mismatch
classification_refusals.why: there is no pairing of labels to scores to score

classification_refusals.name: only_one_class_present
classification_refusals.why: Python's floor, kept here: an input that scores in the browser and refuses on the server is the divergence this contract exists to prevent. It also guarantees both denominators of recall and FPR are non-zero.

classification_refusals.name: label_is_not_zero_or_one
classification_refusals.why: REFUSED IN BOTH LANGUAGES with the same coded InvalidScoreRequest. Python validates binary labels before scikit-learn so neither runtime silently changes the contract.
